sub_answers.sub_question: What are known non-uniqueness and phase transition phenomena for one-dimensional systems with long-range interactions?
Which decidability or algorithmic complexity results concern determining Gibbsianity for given symbolic constraints?
sub_answers.text: The equivalence of conformal measures and Gibbs measures in the sense of the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle equations has been demonstrated for subshifts over a countable group [d57117s0p0]. Decidability of the boundedness problem for monadic least fixed-point recursion based on positive MSO-formulae over trees has been proven, and complexity bounds for this problem have been identified [d23511s0p0]. Decidability of whether a configuration of a pushdown automaton is bisimilar to some finite-state process has been established using first-order grammars and related procedures [d18641s0p0]. Two semantic conditions ensuring decidability of path feasibility in string-manipulating programs have been given, along with a decision procedure and complexity characterizations for the general fragment [d47246s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What limitations exist when extending one-dimensional Gibbs equivalence results to higher dimensions or non-Markovian constraints?
sub_answers.text: Planar defects and disorder perfectly correlated in two dimensions can smear a phase transition in a three-dimensional Ising model so that different parts of the system order at different temperatures and there is no single critical temperature [d137771s0p0]. Rare large impurity-free regions in infinite samples can develop true long-range order while the bulk remains disordered, causing smeared transitions [d137771s0p0]. Duality mappings using two-qubit unitary transformations can transform coupled Hamiltonians into trivial decoupled Hamiltonians, affecting spectral gap scaling and thus limiting naive extensions of one-dimensional equivalences to higher-dimensional many-body settings [d30673s0p0]. Two-particle localization transitions can occur in regimes where single-particle states are localized, and short-range interactions may not change the universality class, which complicates direct generalization of one-dimensional results to interacting higher-dimensional systems [d49563s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What examples demonstrate failure of Gibbsian description for certain g-measures or non-Markovian chains?
How are Gibbs measures used in coding theory and constrained sequence generation for communication systems?
What applications do one-dimensional Gibbs measures have in statistical mechanics and models of spin chains?
sub_answers.text: Infinite-volume Gibbs measures of spin glass models on the hypercube can be identified as random probability measures on the unit ball of a Hilbert space [d3436s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does thermodynamic formalism for symbolic systems impact ergodic theory and entropy calculations?
sub_answers.text: A conformal measure and a Gibbs measure in the sense of the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle equations are equivalent for subshifts over a countable group under a measurable cocycle formulation [d57117s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: In what ways are Gibbs-equivalent descriptions used in statistical inference or hidden Markov modelling?
sub_answers.text: Equivalence between conformal measures and DLR Gibbs measures provides a Gibbs-equivalent description for measures on symbolic subshifts via measurable cocycles [d57117s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What is the definition of a finite-alphabet chain in symbolic dynamics and probability theory?
What are grammar constraints in the context of sequences, including subshifts of finite type and sofic shifts?
sub_answers.text:
Grammar constraints restrict sequences to those generated or recognized by formal grammars such as context-free or linear grammars used to express global constraints on sequences [d5650s0p0].
A GRAMMAR constraint encodes membership of a sequence in the language of a given grammar and can be applied to restricted classes like deterministic, unambiguous, or linear grammars [d5650s0p0].
A subshift of finite type is specified by a finite set of forbidden local patterns and thus enforces sequences avoiding those patterns [d73947s0p0].
A sofic shift is a symbolic dynamical system that can be represented as the image (factor) of a subshift of finite type and can be described by finite-state transducers or labeled graphs [d105143s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What is the definition of a one-dimensional Gibbs measure and its connection to potentials and specifications?
sub_answers.text:
A one-dimensional Gibbs measure can be defined via the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle (DLR) equations as a probability measure satisfying specified conditional probabilities (specifications) consistent with an interaction or potential [d57117s0p0].
A Gibbs measure can alternatively be characterized as a conformal measure associated to a measurable cocycle, and such conformal measures are equivalent to DLR Gibbs measures under appropriate hypotheses [d57117s0p0].
Potentials and interactions induce cocycles or specifications, and one can construct an interaction from a potential (and vice versa) so that they induce the same cocycle defining the Gibbs property [d57117s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are standard equivalence notions between stochastic chains and Gibbs measures in one dimension?
sub_answers.text:
Standard equivalence notions in one dimension include the equivalence between DLR Gibbs measures and conformal measures defined via cocycles [d57117s0p0].
Thermodynamic notions such as existence and uniqueness of invariant ergodic Gibbs measures and uniqueness of equilibrium states are standard equivalence-related criteria connecting stochastic chains and Gibbs measures on shift spaces [d46179s0p0].
Infinite-volume Gibbs measures for lattice models can be identified and studied as limits of finite-volume Gibbs measures and as objects characterized by these equivalence notions [d3436s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What is the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle (DLR) specification condition for Gibbs measures on one-dimensional lattices?
sub_answers.text: The Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle (DLR) specification requires that a measure satisfy conditional distribution equations on finite volumes determined by a measurable cocycle or interaction, so that finite-volume conditional probabilities match the Gibbs specification [d57117s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does the transfer operator (Ruelle operator) characterize Gibbs measures and equilibrium states for symbolic systems?
sub_answers.text: The transfer (Ruelle) operator enters the thermodynamic formalism that characterizes equilibrium states and Gibbs measures for symbolic systems by providing the variational framework for pressure and by producing invariant measures with the Gibbs property [d46179s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What role do summable variations and Bowen regularity of potentials play in uniqueness of Gibbs measures?
sub_answers.text: Summable variation of a potential guarantees that an equilibrium measure is Gibbs for shifts of finite type and yields a topologically Gibbs measure for general subshifts, thereby promoting existence and regularity of Gibbs measures [d4849s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How is equivalence between a stochastic chain and a Gibbs measure established via conditional probabilities or g-functions?
sub_answers.text: Equivalence between a stochastic chain and a Gibbs measure is established by matching finite-volume conditional probabilities of the chain to the Gibbs specification given by a cocycle or interaction, i.e., by verifying the DLR equations for the chain [d57117s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Survey known results on non-uniqueness and phase-transition behavior in one-dimensional lattice systems with long-range interactions: which models (e.g., Dyson Ising with 1/|i-j|^α couplings, Kac-type potentials, power-law Potts chains) exhibit multiple Gibbs measures, at what decay exponents α do transitions occur, and what are the rigorous criteria (Peierls-type bounds, cluster expansion breakdown, fractional moment methods) used to prove them?
sub_answers.text: One-dimensional long-range Ising (Dyson) models with pair potentials ~1/|i-j|^{α} have been studied mainly for slow decays 1<α≤2 and exhibit phase-transition behavior in that regime [d36466s0p0]. Peierls-type contour arguments adapted to long-range interactions provide rigorous proofs of phase transitions for one-dimensional long-range Ising ferromagnets with interactions J(|x-y|)=1/|x-y|^{2-α} for α∈[0,1) [d40221s0p0]. Long-range q-state Potts chains show non-universal critical behavior and require numerical and scaling studies to estimate critical temperatures and exponents, illustrating multiple-measure phenomena in long-range Potts models [d46647s0p0]. Rigorous uniqueness results and analytic control up to spectral thresholds are available for continuum Gibbs point processes via spectral-gap/spectral-threshold methods, providing a contrasting criterion for absence of phase transitions in those settings [d126093s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What decidability and computational-complexity theorems have been proved about the problem ‘given a symbolic constraint or subshift (e.g., a shift of finite type, sofic shift, or a list of forbidden words), decide whether there exists a Gibbs measure consistent with it’: which cases are decidable/undecidable, are there completeness results (RE, co-RE, NP-hard), and what reductions or algorithmic barriers are known?
sub_answers.text: There are proven decidability-style rigorous uniqueness theorems for Gibbs measures in certain settings such as high-temperature uniqueness and analyticity for Euclidean quantum lattice/loop systems and for Gibbs point processes below a spectral threshold, which give algorithmically verifiable conditions in those models [d145643s0p0][d126093s0p0]. Explicit general computability or undecidability classifications (RE/co-RE/NP-hard) for the problem of deciding existence of a Gibbs measure from a symbolic constraint or forbidden-word list are not contained in the cited results and so are not stated here [d35172s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What concrete obstacles and counterexamples prevent the direct extension of one-dimensional equivalence results between Gibbs measures, g-measures, and Markov chains to higher-dimensional lattices or to chains with non-Markovian (infinite-memory) constraints: which technical tools fail (monotonicity/order, transfer-matrix methods, specification-uniqueness arguments), and what negative theorems describe these limitations?
sub_answers.text: One-dimensional techniques that exploit order/monotonicity and transfer-matrix or contour methods permit proofs of phase transition and uniqueness in long-range chains but rely on special one-dimensional adaptations and contour constructions that do not straightforwardly generalize to higher dimensions [d40221s0p0]. Specifications and uniqueness arguments based on summable-variation type conditions can be weakened to Berbee-type conditions in one-sided chains, indicating that some one-dimensional uniqueness tools depend sensitively on variation bounds [d35172s0p0]. Phenomena like pseudo-transitions and extremely large correlation lengths in certain one-dimensional decorated chains show that intuition from short-range one-dimensional uniqueness breaks down in non-Markovian or specially structured models, obstructing direct extension of equivalence results [d45604s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: List canonical counterexample models that show failure of a Gibbsian description for certain g-measures or non-Markovian chains: for instance, descriptions and properties of Bramson–Kalikow constructions, Fernández–Maillard non-Gibbsian chains, Hulse examples, decimations of Gibbs measures and non-continuous conditional probabilities, including what feature (non-quasilocality, essential discontinuity, phase splitting) makes each model non-Gibbsian.
sub_answers.text: Decimation of one-dimensional long-range Gibbs measures can produce non-Gibbsian measures, demonstrating non-quasilocality and essential discontinuities in conditional probabilities after renormalization/decimation [d36466s0p0]. Counterexamples based on one-sided long-range Ising constructions yield sharpness results for conditions ensuring continuous g-functions and produce inverse critical-temperature separations used to show limits of factor maps from Gibbs measures [d35172s0p0]. Known decorated or engineered one-dimensional chains exhibit pseudo-transitions with extremely large correlation lengths and quasi-phase behavior that can be mistaken for genuine phase transitions and thus complicate Gibbs descriptions [d45604s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which specific constructions use Gibbs measures to generate constrained sequences for communication systems (e.g., run-length-limited, (d,k)-constrained, or ISI-avoiding codes), and how are Gibbsian probabilities used to compute channel capacity, design enumerative/biased encoders, or analyze code redundancy and error performance?
sub_answers.text:
Constraint-based codes for DNA storage account explicitly for maximum repetition length and AT/GC balance when constructing constrained sequences [d48005s0p0].
Algorithms exist to compute the number of sequences that satisfy maximum repetition length and AT/GC balance constraints and to translate binary runlength-limited and/or balanced strings into DNA strands [d48005s0p0].
Practical constructions combine maximum repetition length and AT/GC balance and quantify redundancy differences between binary-based routines and fully quaternary approaches [d48005s0p0].
Row-by-row constructions of weakly constrained codes achieve capacity for the weak constraint and have been adapted to be error-resilient, supporting enumerative or structured encoders for constrained sequence sets [d95738s0p0].
Simple capacity computations and design of error-avoidance codes for constrained reader-to-tag channels have been used to guide construction of practical codes for channels with shift-type constraints [d20276s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are concrete roles of one-dimensional Gibbs measures in statistical mechanics models of spin chains (for example the 1D Ising, Potts, classical XY, and quantum XXZ chains): how are Gibbs states, transfer matrices, correlation decay, spectral gap, and exact solutions used to derive thermodynamic quantities and correlation functions?
sub_answers.text:
One-dimensional spin-chain models are analyzed using techniques that yield exact or highly accurate correlation functions and thermodynamic quantities in the thermodynamic limit [d145555s0p0].
The Algebraic Bethe Ansatz is used to construct representations for correlation functions on finite chains and to treat string solutions of Bethe equations in the thermodynamic limit, leading to multiple integral representations for zero-temperature correlation functions [d145555s0p0].
Density matrix renormalization group and quantum information measures (quantum discord, mutual information, coherence) are used to probe quantum and classical correlations and to detect quantum phase transitions and symmetry points in one-dimensional XXZ and bilinear-biquadratic chains [d31144s0p0].
For anisotropic XY spin-1/2 chains in the thermodynamic limit, analytical expressions for classical and quantum pairwise correlations at any distance are obtained and used to study thermal and ground-state behavior [d7435s0p0].
Generalized Gibbsian frameworks establish relative entropy density and equilibrium-state characterizations that connect decaying translation-invariant potentials to thermodynamic descriptions in disordered spin systems [d146055s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: How does the thermodynamic formalism for symbolic dynamical systems—specifically concepts like topological pressure, equilibrium states, the variational principle, and Gibbs measures—affect rigorous ergodic-theoretic results and explicit entropy computations (including entropy rate estimation, large deviations, and multifractal spectra) for shift spaces and subshifts of finite type?
sub_answers.text:
A thermodynamic formalism for generalized Gibbs measures establishes existence of relative entropy density and expresses it in terms of entropy and relative energy for almost Gibbsian measures [d146055s0p0].
These measures can be characterized as equilibrium states and the usual variational principle can be extended to cover almost Gibbsian and quasilocal measures, yielding rigorous links between Gibbsian descriptions and entropy/energy tradeoffs [d146055s0p0].
For joint measures of disordered spin systems, weak Gibbs properties with rapidly decaying potentials can hold, and loss of the almost Gibbs property leads to failure of the variational principle, affecting rigorous entropy and equilibrium analyses [d146055s0p0].
Row-by-row constructions of weakly constrained codes can achieve the capacity of a weak constraint, connecting symbolic constrained systems to explicit entropy-capacity computations in shift-like spaces [d95738s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What literature and algorithms describe the relationships and conversions between Gibbs descriptions and statistical-inference models such as hidden Markov models or Markov random fields—for example equivalence conditions, parameter estimation methods (MLE, EM, pseudolikelihood), identifiability issues, and practical inference algorithms that exploit Gibbs/HMM duality?

Give a precise mathematical definition of a finite-alphabet chain as used in symbolic dynamics and probability theory: specify the index set (Z or N), the finite alphabet, the product/shift space and sigma‑algebra, what is meant by a stochastic chain or shift‑invariant process on that space, and typical examples (Markov chains, stationary processes, shift‑invariant measures).
sub_answers.text:
A finite-alphabet chain is a stochastic process indexed by the integers or the natural numbers taking values in a finite set called the alphabet, realized as a shift space with the product topology and the product σ-algebra on sequences over that alphabet [d22204s0p0][d62325s0p0].
A shift-invariant process on this space is a probability measure on the sequence space that is invariant under the left (or right) shift map, and stationary processes and shift-invariant measures are standard examples of such chains [d74977s0p0][d22204s0p0].
Typical examples include finite-state Markov chains and higher-order Markov chains (finite-order dependence), and variable-length Markov chains described by context trees, each admitting questions of existence and uniqueness of stationary probability measures [d62325s0p0][d44909s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Explain what is meant by grammar or constraint descriptions for sequences: define forbidden words and the language of a shift, characterize subshifts of finite type via finite sets of forbidden blocks and via adjacency/transition matrices, and describe sofic shifts via labeled finite graphs and resulting factor maps; include the equivalent combinatorial, topological, and presentation-based definitions.
sub_answers.text:
Grammar or constraint descriptions for sequences are given by forbidding finite blocks (forbidden words), and the language of a shift is the set of all finite words that appear in its sequences; a subshift is defined by specifying which finite words are forbidden from appearing [d73947s0p0].
A subshift of finite type is characterized by a finite set of forbidden blocks and can equivalently be presented by a finite adjacency or transition matrix encoding allowed successive symbols [d73947s0p0].
A sofic shift is the image (factor) of a shift of finite type and can be presented by a labeled finite directed graph or finite-state transducer, with the labeled graph producing the sofic language and the factor map given by the labeling; such presentation-based, combinatorial, and topological descriptions are equivalent ways to define sofic shifts [d105143s0p0][d28674s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: State the definition of a one‑dimensional Gibbs measure in rigorous terms: give the form of potentials/interactions (finite‑range, summable), define the Gibbsian specification or family of conditional probabilities (DLR equations), show how the potential determines the specification and vice versa, and mention common equivalent formulations (Boltzmann weights, Hamiltonians, transfer operator/Markov kernel representations).

List and define the standard notions used to compare stochastic chains and Gibbs measures in one dimension: equivalence as the same invariant measure, being Gibbs for the same potential or for equivalent specifications, Markov/Gibbs correspondence (finite‑range potentials ↔ finite‑order Markov chains), g‑measures versus Gibbs measures, conditions like continuity or summable variation, Dobrushin/uniqueness criteria, and classifications such as measure conjugacy or factor maps that relate chains and Gibbs states.

Formulate the Dobrushin–Lanford–Ruelle (DLR) specification for Gibbs measures on a one-dimensional lattice (Z or N): express the finite-volume conditional probability kernels, the consistency (specification) property across increasing intervals, and how boundary conditions appear in the DLR equations.
sub_answers.text:
Finite-volume conditional probability kernels are specified by requiring that the conditional law on a finite interval equals the Gibbs specification kernel determined by a cocycle or interaction given the exterior configuration as boundary condition [d57117s0p0].
The DLR consistency property demands that these finite-volume kernels form a coherent specification across increasing intervals, so conditioning first on a larger interval and then on a subinterval yields the same conditional probabilities as conditioning directly on the subinterval [d57117s0p0].
Boundary conditions enter the DLR equations through the exterior configuration which appears in the measurable cocycle or interaction that defines the finite-volume conditional kernels [d57117s0p0].
A measure satisfies the DLR equations if and only if its finite-volume conditional distributions agree with the specified kernels for all finite intervals and almost every external boundary configuration [d57117s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Explain how the transfer (Ruelle–Perron–Frobenius) operator is used to identify Gibbs measures and equilibrium states on symbolic spaces (full shift and subshifts of finite type): include the role of leading eigenfunction/eigenmeasure, normalization to a conformal measure, and the relation to topological pressure and variational principle.
sub_answers.text:
The transfer (Ruelle–Perron–Frobenius) operator identifies Gibbs measures by admitting a leading eigenvalue together with a corresponding leading eigenfunction and eigenmeasure, whose product yields an invariant Gibbs state or equilibrium measure on the symbolic space [d32627s0p0].
Normalization of the leading eigenmeasure against the eigenfunction produces a conformal measure which satisfies the conformality relation induced by the potential and cocycle [d32627s0p0][d57117s0p0].
The leading eigenvalue of the Ruelle operator is related to the topological pressure, and the variational principle links this pressure to equilibrium states which are realized by the Gibbs measures constructed from the leading eigenfunction and eigenmeasure [d32627s0p0][d4849s0p0].
These spectral objects can be used to prove existence and uniqueness of Gibbs/equilibrium measures on full shifts and certain subshifts when the operator has the appropriate spectral properties [d32627s0p0][d46179s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Describe precisely how regularity conditions on a potential—such as summable variations, Walters' condition, Bowen regularity, or Hölder continuity—control uniqueness (or nonuniqueness) of Gibbs measures on one-dimensional shifts, and give the specific hypotheses and counterexamples that distinguish uniqueness regimes (e.g., exponential vs. merely summable decay).
sub_answers.text:
Regularity conditions such as d-summable variation, Walters' condition, Bowen regularity, or Hölder continuity control uniqueness of Gibbs measures by ensuring sufficient decay of variation so that classical theorems guarantee that equilibrium measures are Gibbs and uniqueness holds in strong regularity regimes [d4849s0p0][d32627s0p0].
Exponential (e.g., Hölder) decay of variations typically yields uniqueness of the Gibbs/equilibrium state via spectral gap properties of the Ruelle operator, whereas merely summable decay can permit nonuniqueness or multiple eigenobjects in marginal cases [d32627s0p0][d4849s0p0].
Concrete counterexamples to uniqueness arise for less regular potentials on countable or coded shifts where multiple Gibbs-like measures or different eigenfunctions/eigenmeasures can coexist despite summable but nonexponential decay [d32627s0p0][d129586s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: State the criteria and construction that establish equivalence between a stochastic chain with complete connections (a g-chain) and a Gibbs measure: define g-functions or normalized conditional kernels, non-nullness and continuity requirements, and the proof sketch showing that a consistent family of one-sided conditional probabilities yields a two-sided DLR Gibbs measure (and conversely).
sub_answers.text:
Equivalence between a stochastic chain with complete connections (a g-chain) and a Gibbs measure is established by defining a normalized g-function that gives one-sided conditional kernels which are strictly positive (non-nullness) and continuous in the conditioning configuration [d74038s0p0].
Non-nullness and continuity of the g-function guarantee that the family of finite-dimensional conditional probabilities is consistent and extends to a shift-invariant two-sided measure satisfying DLR-type equations with the same cocycle [d74038s0p0][d57117s0p0].
Conversely, a Gibbs measure specified by a measurable cocycle or interaction yields normalized one-sided conditional kernels (g-functions) so that the two descriptions coincide when the cocycle admits the corresponding normalized conditional probabilities [d57117s0p0][d74038s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What specific instances and rigorous criteria are known for non-uniqueness and phase-transition behavior in one-dimensional lattice models with long-range interactions (e.g., Ising-type models with power-law decay J(r) ~ r^{-α}): which decay exponents, interaction classes, or boundary conditions produce multiple Gibbs states or fail uniqueness?
sub_answers.text:
One-dimensional Ising ferromagnets with pair potentials decaying as |i-j|^{-α} display phase transitions and non-uniqueness for slow decays in the range 1 < α ≤ 2 at low temperature [d36466s0p0].
Decimation (a renormalization) of such one-dimensional long-range Gibbs measures can produce non-Gibbsian measures, showing failure of uniqueness under that transformation [d36466s0p0].
In one-dimensional quantum anharmonic crystal models with attractive interaction and one-dimensional oscillations, the set of Gibbs measures is non-singleton at low temperatures, demonstrating phase coexistence in one dimension under those conditions [d145643s0p0].
Uniqueness of Gibbs measures holds at high temperatures and under nonzero external field or strong quantum diffusivity in the quantum anharmonic crystal setting [d145643s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are the precise decidability and computational-complexity results about determining whether a given symbolic specification or finite-range constraint defines a Gibbsian measure (or is Gibbs-equivalent to some finite-range potential)? Include known undecidability results, complexity classes, and positive algorithms for one-dimensional subshifts, Markov chains, or g-functions.

Which structural obstructions and counterexamples prevent the one-dimensional equivalence theorems (e.g., between Markov chains, Gibbs measures, and g-measures) from carrying over to higher dimensions or to non-Markovian (infinite-memory) constraints — specifically, what assumptions break (e.g., Perron–Frobenius, summability, continuity) and what general negative results are proven?
sub_answers.text:
Non-uniqueness and contested phase structure arise when long-range power-law interactions decay slowly (e.g., 1 < α ≤ 2), which violates conditions that guarantee uniqueness in short-range or rapidly decaying systems [d36466s0p0].
Failure of uniqueness also occurs in models where quantum effects are weak at low temperature and interactions are attractive, breaking strong-diffusivity-induced uniqueness [d145643s0p0].
Contested organizational descriptions of phases in higher-dimensional disordered systems stem from debates over whether multiple incongruent Gibbs states exist, as reflected in analyses of free-energy-difference fluctuations and metastates for spin glasses [d98617s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Give concrete, referenced examples of stochastic chains or g-measures that cannot be represented as Gibbs measures (or whose Gibbs description fails): name constructions (e.g., Bramson–Kalikow-type nonunique g-functions, decimation or renormalization examples producing non-Gibbsian measures, explicit chains with discontinuous conditional probabilities) and summarize the mechanism by which Gibbsianity fails.
sub_answers.text:
Decimation (a renormalization transformation) of one-dimensional Dyson-type long-range Gibbs measures produces explicit examples of measures that become non-Gibbsian after the transformation [d36466s0p0].
Renormalization/decimation mechanisms lead to non-Gibbsianity by creating conditional probabilities with pathological (discontinuous or nonlocal) dependence on boundary conditions in the transformed measure [d36466s0p0].
In quantum anharmonic crystal models, low-temperature attractive interactions give rise to multiple Gibbs measures, providing concrete models where a simple Gibbs description is non-unique or fails to single out a unique equilibrium state [d145643s0p0].
Analyses of spin-glass free-energy-difference fluctuations produce constructions and arguments relevant to incongruent Gibbs states and to measures whose Gibbs description is contested due to complex organization of pure and mixed states [d98617s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Which specific coding-theory constructions and constrained sequence encoders (e.g., run-length-limited codes, constrained sequence compressors, or sliding-block codes) explicitly use Gibbs distributions or Markov/Gibbs measures, and what performance gains or error-rate bounds do these measures provide in communication channels?

What concrete examples of one-dimensional Gibbs measures arise in statistical mechanics models such as the Ising chain, Potts chain, and Dyson long-range models, and how are they used to derive correlation decay, phase transition behavior, and explicit solution methods for these spin-chain systems?

How does the thermodynamic formalism for subshifts of finite type or countable-state symbolic dynamics (pressure, equilibrium states, transfer operators) translate into tools for proving results in ergodic theory, computing metric/topological entropy, and establishing variational principles for invariant measures?
sub_answers.text: A measure satisfying the Dobrushin-Lanford-Ruelle equations must be conformal with respect to a measurable cocycle [d57117s0p0]. The DLR equations can be formulated more generally with respect to a measurable cocycle that reduces to the classical equations when the cocycle is induced by an interaction or a potential [d57117s0p0]. Methods exist to construct an interaction from a potential and vice versa so that the constructed interaction and potential induce the same cocycle, ensuring consistency of the formalism [d57117s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: What are the practical roles of Gibbs-equivalent representations (e.g., exponential family, Gibbs sampler, or pseudo-likelihood approximations) in statistical inference for hidden Markov models and in learning latent-variable graphical models, including parameter estimation, model selection, and approximation error guarantees?

Provide a formal definition of a finite-alphabet chain as used in symbolic dynamics and probability theory: specify the underlying finite alphabet, the space of bi-infinite or one-sided symbol sequences, the shift transformation, typical topologies and sigma-algebras, and how a stochastic process on that alphabet is represented as a measure on the shift space; include basic examples (finite-state Markov chains, i.i.d. processes) and key properties used in the literature.
sub_answers.text:
A finite alphabet is a finite set of symbols used to form words and sequences [d11240s0p0][d2478s0p0].
The space of one-sided or two-sided symbol sequences is a shift space consisting of sequences over the finite alphabet, with both one-sided and two-sided shift variants studied (e.g., one-sided and two-sided Dyck shifts) [d146331s0p0].
The shift transformation acts by moving symbols along the sequence and shift-invariant measures on these spaces are central objects of study [d146331s0p0][d74977s0p0].
A stochastic chain on a finite alphabet can be represented by a probability measure on the shift space that assigns probabilities to cylinder sets of symbol sequences, including chains of variable memory length where a finite suffix (context) of the past suffices to predict the next symbol [d2478s0p0][d74977s0p0].
Basic examples include stochastic chains with memory of variable length defined by finite contexts and finite-state Markov processes that appear in applications to reversible Markov processes [d2478s0p0][d40797s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Define and characterize grammar constraints on sequences: explain forbidden-word descriptions and transition rules, give the precise definition of a subshift of finite type (SFT) via a finite set of forbidden blocks and via a finite adjacency matrix, and define sofic shifts as images (factors) of SFTs or via labeled finite-state automata; include examples and note how these constraints determine admissible sequences and languages.
sub_answers.text:
Grammar constraints on sequences can be described by forbidden words or by transition rules that restrict which finite blocks may appear in admissible sequences [d11240s0p0][d131776s0p0].
A subshift of finite type (SFT) can be specified by a finite set of forbidden blocks or equivalently by a finite adjacency matrix that encodes allowed transitions between symbols or blocks [d34957s0p0][d131776s0p0].
Sofic shifts are factors (images) of SFTs and can be described by labeled finite-state automata that generate the admissible language [d131776s0p0].
Concrete constrained examples include symbolic shifts arising from formal languages such as the Dyck shift, whose admissible sequences are determined by its syntactic constraints [d146331s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Give the definition of a one-dimensional Gibbs measure: specify the role of a potential (interaction/pairwise or finite-range potential), the construction of the specification or conditional probabilities (DLR equations) on finite intervals, and how a Gibbs measure is a probability measure consistent with that specification; also state common regularity conditions on the potential (summable variations, Hölder continuity) and explain links to transfer operators and invariant measures.

List and explain the standard equivalence and comparison notions between stochastic chains on a one-dimensional alphabet and Gibbs measures: include definitions and relations among finite-order Markov chains, chains with complete connections (g-measures), Gibbs measures (DLR), and equilibrium states; state known criteria and theorems that give equivalence or non-equivalence (e.g., summable variation or continuity conditions, uniqueness vs non-uniqueness, existence via thermodynamic formalism, examples where a g-measure is not Gibbs and vice versa).
sub_answers.text:
Finite-order Markov chains and chains with variable-length memory are both classes of stochastic chains studied on one-dimensional symbol spaces, with variable-length chains characterized by finite contexts that predict the next symbol [d2478s0p0].
Shift-invariant measures can be constructed for symbolic systems arising from substitutions and related dynamics, yielding both finite and infinite invariant measures in these settings [d74977s0p0].
Unique tail-invariant and shift-invariant probability measures arise in some constrained shifts, for example the one-sided Dyck shift has a unique tail-invariant topologically σ-finite measure which is a shift-invariant probability and is one of the measures of maximal entropy [d146331s0p0].
Connections between stochastic chains and invariant or equilibrium measures are used in applications to reversible Markov processes and to realizations of stochastic processes from covariance kernels [d40797s0p0][d74977s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Give a precise statement of the Dobrushin–Lanford–Ruelle (DLR) specification condition for Gibbs measures on the one-dimensional integer lattice Z: define the specification kernels (conditional probabilities) for finite intervals, the compatibility (consistency) requirement with respect to conditioning on outside configurations, and the quasilocality (or continuity) condition used in 1D results; include how boundary conditions and finite-volume Gibbs measures converge to DLR measures.
sub_answers.text:
For Z one defines specification kernels as finite-volume conditional probability kernels giving for each finite interval Λ⊂Z and each exterior configuration η the probability measure on configurations in Λ conditioned on η outside Λ; [d57117s0p0].
These finite-volume Gibbs measures are required to be compatible in that conditioning a finite-volume conditional probability on a larger outside set yields the same kernel as conditioning stepwise, i.e., the family of kernels satisfies the DLR consistency equations with respect to the chosen cocycle or interaction; [d57117s0p0].
Quasilocality is imposed as continuity of the finite-volume conditional probabilities in the exterior configuration in the product topology, ensuring conditional probabilities depend weakly on distant boundary changes; [d4849s0p0].
Convergence to DLR measures is obtained by taking limits of finite-volume Gibbs measures with specified boundary conditions along increasing sequences of intervals (van Hove sequences in one dimension), and any limiting measure that satisfies the consistency (DLR) equations and quasilocality is a Gibbs (DLR) measure; [d57117s0p0][d4849s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Explain how the Ruelle (transfer) operator characterizes Gibbs measures and equilibrium states for symbolic dynamical systems: define the operator for a given potential on a full shift or subshift of finite type, state the Ruelle–Perron–Frobenius theorem (existence of leading eigenfunction and eigenmeasure), and show how eigenpairs produce invariant Gibbs/equilibrium measures and satisfy the variational principle for pressure.
sub_answers.text:
For a symbolic system with a potential φ, the Ruelle transfer operator L_φ acts on observables f by (L_φ f)(x)=Σ_{y:σ(y)=x} e^{φ(y)} f(y), defined on a full shift or subshift of finite type; [d4849s0p0][d46179s0p0].
The Ruelle–Perron–Frobenius theorem guarantees a leading eigenvalue, a positive continuous eigenfunction, and an eigenmeasure for L_φ under regularity hypotheses, yielding an eigenpair (h,ν) with L_φ h=λ h and L_φ^* ν=λ ν; [d4849s0p0][d46179s0p0].
Normalizing the eigenpair produces an invariant probability measure μ=h ν which is a Gibbs/equilibrium state for φ and attains the topological pressure, thereby linking the spectral data of L_φ to the variational principle for pressure; [d4849s0p0][d46179s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: State precise definitions and theorems relating regularity conditions on potentials — e.g., summable variation, Walters condition, Bowen regularity — to uniqueness (or nonuniqueness) of Gibbs measures on one-dimensional symbolic spaces: give the definition of variation_n(φ), the summable-variation criterion, examples of potentials that satisfy Bowen or Walters conditions, and explicit uniqueness results and known counterexamples when these conditions fail.
sub_answers.text:
Variation_n(φ) is defined as the supremum of |φ(x)-φ(y)| over pairs x,y that agree on coordinates -n..n, and summable-variation means Σ_n variation_n(φ)<∞; [d4849s0p0].
If φ has d-summable variation (summable variation in the relevant metric) then for shifts of finite type any equilibrium measure is Gibbs and uniqueness of the Gibbs measure follows under those summable-variation hypotheses; [d4849s0p0].
Walters and Bowen regularity are stronger continuity constraints on φ that imply summable variation and hence uniqueness of Gibbs/equilibrium measures in many one-dimensional symbolic settings, while failure of these regularity conditions can produce nonuniqueness and counterexamples on more general subshifts; [d4849s0p0][d46179s0p0].

sub_answers.sub_question: Formulate the equivalence (and differences) between stochastic chains with complete connections / g-measures and DLR Gibbs measures: define a g-function (regular conditional probability) and its compatibility equation, show how a g-measure yields a DLR specification and vice versa under continuity/regularity hypotheses, and cite criteria (e.g., non-nullness, continuity, summable variation) ensuring existence and uniqueness of the corresponding Gibbs measure.
sub_answers.text:
A g-function is a regular conditional probability g(x_0 | x_{-∞}^{-1}) giving probabilities of the next symbol given the past and satisfying the normalization and compatibility equation that integrates to the one-step transition law; [d146055s0p0].
A g-measure is a stationary measure whose one-step conditional probabilities agree almost surely with a given g-function, and such a g-measure induces a DLR specification by using the g-function to define finite-interval conditionals consistent with the DLR equations under continuity hypotheses; [d146055s0p0][d57117s0p0].
Non-nullness together with continuity or summable-variation of the g-function ensures existence and can imply uniqueness of the corresponding Gibbs/DLR measure, while loss of these regularity properties can lead to nonuniqueness or generalized (weak/ almost) Gibbs behaviour; [d146055s0p0][d4849s0p0]
